entry: American [[Track and field|track and field]] athlete, known as Flo-Jo. She set world records in the 100 m and 200 m in 1988 and won three gold medals at the 1988 Olympics. She had qualified for the 1980 Olympics but did not compete due to the U.S. boycott, and she won a silver medal in the 200 m at the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles. She graduated from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1983 with a bachelor's degree in [[Psychology|psychology]]. In February 1989 she abruptly retired and remained a pop culture figure through endorsements, acting and design work. Some contemporaries, including [[Carl Lewis]], voiced doping suspicions without supporting evidence; she passed every drug test administered, with no positive results recorded.

City (pop., 2026: 361,625), capital of [[Tuscany]], Italy. Founded as a Roman garrison in 59 BC, Florence was one of the wealthiest cities of medieval Europe through trade and finance, and many academics consider it the birthplace of the [[Renaissance]]. From 1865 to 1871 it was the capital of the [[Kingdom of Italy]]. The Florentine dialect forms the base of standard Italian, owing to the prestige of works by [[Dante Alighieri]] and [[Petrarch]]. [[UNESCO]] declared the Historic Centre of Florence a World Heritage Site in 1982, and the [[Uffizi|Uffizi Gallery]] and Palazzo Pitti draw millions of visitors each year.

State in the southeastern United States, occupying a peninsula between the [[Gulf of Mexico]] and the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States, about 1,350 miles (2,170 km), and is the only state bordering both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. With a population of over 23 million, it is the third-most populous state. In 1513 Spanish explorer [[Juan Ponce de León]] became the first European to land in the region, and St. Augustine, founded in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States. Florida was admitted as the 27th state on March 3, 1845, and seceded from the Union on January 10, 1861. Its economy is the fourth largest of any U.S. state, led by [[Tourism|tourism]], and attractions such as [[Walt Disney World]] and the [[Kennedy Space Center]] draw tens of millions of visitors annually.

Powder made by grinding grains, [[Bean|beans]], [[Nut (fruit)|nuts]], [[Seed|seeds]], roots or [[Vegetable|vegetables]], used in baked goods and to thicken dishes. Cereal flour, particularly wheat flour, is the main ingredient of [[Bread|bread]], a staple food for many cultures; archaeologists have found evidence of humans making cereal flour over 32,000 years ago. Whole-grain flour retains the endosperm, germ and bran, while refined flour is endosperm alone. Refining removes nutrients, so white flour may be fortified, and as of 2016 it was a legal requirement in 86 countries to fortify wheat flour. Nut flour is a popular gluten-free alternative used in the keto and paleo diets. [[Cassava|Cassava flour]] is also gluten-free, and [[Chickpea|chickpea]] flour, or gram flour, is traditional in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Indian cuisine.

Diagram that represents a workflow or process. Steps are drawn as boxes connected by arrows that show their order, with rectangles for activities and diamonds for decisions. A flowchart is a diagrammatic representation of an [[Algorithm|algorithm]] and is used to analyze, design, document or manage processes. Frank and Lillian Gilbreth introduced the first structured method for documenting process flow in 1921. In 1947 [[John von Neumann|John von Neumann]] and Herman Goldstine adapted flowcharts to represent algorithms for early electronic computers. ISO published standard 5807 in 1985.

[[Clade|Clade]] of seed plants that bear flowers and fruits, also called angiosperms. Angiosperms are by far the most diverse group of land plants, with 64 orders, 416 families, approximately 13,000 known genera and 300,000 known species. They are distinguished from [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]] by having flowers, vessel elements in their xylem, endosperm within their seeds, and fruits that completely envelop the seeds. They diversified explosively in the [[Cretaceous]] and became the dominant plants across the planet. Agriculture depends almost entirely on flowering plants; [[Rice]], [[Maize]] and [[Wheat]] provide half of the world's staple calorie intake. Many flowering plants are threatened by habitat destruction and by [[Climate change|climate change]].

1979 Gothic novel by V. C. Andrews, the first book in the Dollanganger series. Narrated by Cathy Dollanganger, it tells how she and three siblings are hidden in an attic room of Foxworth Hall, a mansion in [[Virginia]], under the control of their mother and grandmother. The novel was popular but controversial for its depictions of abuse and sexual content. It was twice adapted into films, in 1987 and 2014.

American professional boxer and [[Boxing|boxing]] promoter, undefeated at 50–0. He won 15 major world championships across five weight classes, including the *Ring* magazine title in three weight classes. As an amateur he won a bronze medal in the featherweight division at the 1996 Olympics. He retired from professional boxing in August 2017 and moved to exhibition bouts. In 2018 he was the highest-paid athlete in the world, with earnings of $285 million according to [[Forbes]]. He shares with [[Joe Louis]] the record of 26 consecutive wins in world title fights, and he founded Mayweather Promotions in 2006.

Subdiscipline of [[Fluid mechanics|fluid mechanics]] concerned with the flow of liquids and gases. Its subdisciplines include [[Aerodynamics|aerodynamics]], the study of air and other gases in motion, and hydrodynamics, the study of water and other liquids in motion. Applications include calculating forces and moments on [[Aircraft|aircraft]], determining the mass flow rate of [[Petroleum|petroleum]] through [[Pipeline|pipelines]], predicting weather patterns and modeling fission weapon detonation. Its foundational axioms are the [[Conservation of mass|conservation of mass]], of linear momentum and of energy, based on [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]]. For Newtonian fluids the momentum equations are the [[Navier–Stokes equations|Navier–Stokes equations]]; the unsimplified form has no general closed-form solution, so it is mainly used in computational fluid dynamics.

Branch of physics concerned with the mechanics of liquids, gases and plasmas, and the forces on them. Originally applied to water, it is used in mechanical, aerospace, civil, chemical and biomedical engineering, as well as [[Geophysics|geophysics]], [[Oceanography|oceanography]], [[Meteorology|meteorology]], [[Astrophysics|astrophysics]] and biology. It is divided into fluid statics, the study of fluids at rest, and [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]], the study of the effect of forces on fluid motion. It is a branch of [[Continuum mechanics|continuum mechanics]], which models matter from a macroscopic viewpoint rather than as atoms. Archimedes investigated fluid statics and buoyancy in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], and [[Daniel Bernoulli|Daniel Bernoulli]] introduced mathematical fluid dynamics in *Hydrodynamica* (1739).

One of two kinds of photoluminescence, in which a substance emits light after absorbing [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]]. Ultraviolet exposure makes many substances glow with [[Color|colored]] visible light, the color depending on their chemical composition. Fluorescent materials generally stop glowing almost immediately when the radiation stops, which distinguishes them from phosphorescence. The emitted light may have a longer [[Wavelength|wavelength]] than the absorbed radiation, so invisible [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light can produce a visible glow. Fluorescence has many practical applications, including [[Mineralogy|mineralogy]], [[Medicine|medicine]], chemical sensors, fluorescent labeling and cosmic-ray detection. Its most common everyday use is in fluorescent lamps and LED lamps, where coatings convert ultraviolet or blue light into white light.

[[Chemical element]] (symbol F; atomic number 9), the lightest [[Halogen|halogen]]. At standard conditions it is a pale yellow diatomic gas, extremely reactive with all elements except the light noble gases, and highly toxic in elemental form. Elemental fluorine was first isolated in 1886 by French chemist Henri Moissan using low-temperature [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]], a process still used in production. Industrial production for uranium enrichment began during the [[Manhattan Project]] in World War II. Because pure fluorine is costly to refine, most commercial uses involve compounds; about half of mined [[Fluorite|fluorite]] is used in steelmaking. Organofluorine compounds serve as refrigerants, electrical insulation and [[Polytetrafluoroethylene|PTFE]] (Teflon). Fluoride ions inhibit [[Tooth decay|dental cavities]] and are used in toothpaste and water fluoridation.

Mineral form of [[Calcium|calcium]] fluoride, CaF₂, also called fluorspar. It typically forms cubic crystals and has a [[Mohs scale|Mohs hardness]] of 4. Pure fluorite is colorless and transparent, but impurities usually make it colorful. It is used as a flux in [[Smelting|smelting]] and in making certain [[Glass|glasses]] and enamels. Its purest grades supply fluoride for [[Hydrofluoric acid|hydrofluoric acid]]. Optically clear fluorite is used in apochromatic lenses. The name derives from the Latin *fluere*, meaning to flow.

Mixture of [[Hydrogen fluoride|hydrogen fluoride]] and antimony pentafluoride. It is the strongest known superacid, stronger than pure [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]] by many orders of magnitude on the Hammett acidity function. Its lowest attained value of that function (H₀) is about −28, although some sources report values below −31. Its extreme acidity comes from the fluoronium ion, H₂F⁺, which forms when hydrogen fluoride accepts a proton. It protonates some [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]] to form carbocations and attacks glass, so it is stored in containers lined with PTFE (Teflon).

[[Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor|Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor]] (SSRI) antidepressant, sold as Prozac among others. Used to treat [[Major depressive disorder|major depressive disorder]], [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive–compulsive disorder]], panic disorder, [[Bulimia|bulimia nervosa]] and premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Common side effects include loss of appetite, nausea, [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]] and sexual dysfunction. Serious side effects include serotonin syndrome, mania, seizures, an increased risk of suicidal behavior and an increased risk of bleeding. Eli Lilly invented it in 1972, and it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. In 2024 it was the nineteenth most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 29 million prescriptions.

Woodwind instrument whose sound is produced by air blown across an opening. Flutes are aerophones, classified as edge-blown in the Hornbostel–Sachs system, and a player is called a flautist or flutist. Paleolithic flutes with hand-bored holes, dating to about 53,000 to 45,000 years ago, have been found in the Swabian Jura region of present-day [[Germany|Germany]] and are the earliest known identifiable musical instruments. The [[Bamboo|bamboo]] flute has a long history in [[China|China]] and [[India|India]], where the cross flute was sacred to [[Krishna|Krishna]]. Transverse flutes entered [[Europe|Europe]] through Byzantium and were depicted in Greek art about 800 AD. The modern concert flute is typically made of [[Silver|silver]] or nickel and has a range of about three octaves.

Concept in [[Applied mathematics|applied mathematics]] with many applications in physics, describing an effect that appears to pass through a surface or substance. For transport phenomena such as [[Heat transfer|heat transfer]] and [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]], flux is the rate of flow of a property per unit area, a vector quantity. In [[Vector calculus|vector calculus]], it is a scalar quantity defined as the surface integral of the perpendicular component of a vector field over a surface. The word comes from the Latin *fluxus*, meaning flow, and [[Isaac Newton|Isaac Newton]] introduced it into [[Differential calculus|differential calculus]] as fluxion. [[Joseph Fourier|Joseph Fourier]] made heat flux a key concept in his analysis of heat transfer.

[[Insect|Insect]] of the order Diptera, named for its single pair of wings. Flies undergo complete [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]], and their larvae often develop inside the food source. The order contains more than 150,000 species, including horseflies, crane flies, hoverflies and mosquitoes. Flies are major [[Pollination|pollinators]], second only to bees and their hymenopteran relatives. Fruit flies are used as [[Model organism|model organisms]] in research, while mosquitoes transmit malaria, dengue, yellow fever and West Nile fever. Houseflies spread [[Foodborne illness|foodborne illnesses]], and dipteran larvae, known as maggots, are used as fishing bait and in medical debridement to clean wounds.

Family of saltwater ray-finned fish, with about 64 [[Species|species]] in seven [[Genus|genera]]. Their long, wing-like paired fins act as aerofoils that generate lift, enabling powerful leaps and prolonged glides over considerable distances above the surface. The leaps are thought to help them escape underwater predators such as [[Swordfish|swordfish]], mackerel, tuna and marlin, though they expose them to aerial predators such as [[Frigatebird|frigatebirds]]. Flying fish live in all oceans, particularly in tropical and warm subtropical waters, and are commonly found in the upper 200 m (660 ft) of the [[Ocean|ocean]]. [[Barbados]] is known as "the land of the flying fish", and the French Exocet anti-ship missile is named after them.

Two-phase material consisting of [[Gas|gas]] cells dispersed in a continuous [[Liquid|liquid]] or [[Solid|solid]] phase. In most foams the gas occupies most of the volume, divided into bubbles separated by thin films. Liquid and solid foams differ in formation and structure, and solid foams may be open-celled or closed-celled. Foams form when gas is dispersed into a liquid or solid, typically with surfactants that reduce [[Surface tension|surface tension]]; their stability depends on surface tension, drainage and gas diffusion. Applications include thermal insulation, packaging, flotation devices, fire retardant foams and froth flotation. Common examples are [[Soap|soap]] foam, the head on beer, [[Bread|bread]] and bath sponges.

Measure of how strongly an optical system converges or diverges [[Light|light]]. For an idealized thin [[Lens|lens]], it is the distance between the lens and its [[Focus (optics)|focal points]]. A positive focal length means the system converges light, and a negative one means it diverges light. For a thin lens, the focal length f, object distance u and image distance v are related by 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. In most [[Photography|photography]] and all [[Telescope|telescopy]], a longer focal length gives higher magnification and a narrower angle of view. In microscopy, where the object is brought close to the lens, a shorter focal length gives higher magnification. For more general systems, the effective focal length is the inverse of the optical power and is used to calculate magnification.

Point at which light rays originating from a point on an object converge. Because a focus has physical extent, it forms a blur circle, and [[Diffraction|diffraction]] sets the smallest possible blur circle, the Airy disc, even without aberrations. An image is in focus when light from object points is converged almost as much as possible. For a [[Lens|lens]] or spherical or parabolic mirror, the principal focus is the point onto which collimated light parallel to the axis is focused. A lens has two focal points, one on each side, and the distance from the lens to its focus is the [[Focal length|focal length]]. A hyperbolic mirror can focus rays aimed at the focal point behind it toward the one in front, as in a Cassegrain telescope.

Visible [[Aerosol|aerosol]] of tiny water droplets or ice crystals held in the air near the Earth's surface. Fog is a type of low-lying [[Cloud|cloud]], usually resembling stratus, and by definition reduces visibility to less than 1 km (0.62 mi). Fog forms when water vapor condenses, which happens when the difference between air temperature and the [[Dew point|dew point]] is less than 2.5 °C (4.5 °F). Sea fog forms as water vapor condenses on bits of salt. Its moisture is often generated locally, from nearby water, marshes or moist ground, and fog affects shipping, travel and warfare. Fog commonly produces [[Precipitation|precipitation]] in the form of drizzle or very light snow, and its droplets host bacteria that actively grow and divide.

Specialty food made from the [[Liver|liver]] of a duck or goose fattened by *gavage*, or force-feeding. French law defines *foie gras* this way, and it is prized for a rich, [[Butter|buttery]] flavor. It is sold whole or prepared as mousse, *parfait* or *pâté*, and is a delicacy in [[French cuisine|French cuisine]]. The practice dates to [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] around 2500 BC. France is by far the largest producer and consumer. Production is controversial over animal welfare concerns, and several countries have laws against force-feeding and against producing or selling it.

Stack of originally planar surfaces, such as sedimentary strata, bent during permanent deformation. Folds range from microscopic crinkles to mountain-sized structures, occurring singly or in periodic sets called fold trains. They form under varied stress, pore pressure and temperature, and are found in soft sediments and across the full spectrum of [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rocks]]. Folds are commonly formed by shortening of existing layers, but they also form from displacement on a non-planar [[Fault (geology)|fault]]. A regional set of folds makes up a fold belt, a common feature of orogenic zones. The fold hinge is the line joining points of maximum curvature, and the limbs are the flanks of the fold. Gentle folds have an interlimb angle between 180° and 120°, while tight folds lie between 30° and 0°.
